nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the vernacular novel, the travel book and the tall tale
literary_identity: Novelist, humorist and travel writer; the author of Adventures of Huckleberry Finn and the founder of the American vernacular prose style.
biography: Born Samuel Langhorne Clemens in Florida, Missouri, on 30 November 1835 and brought up in Hannibal on the Mississippi; he was apprenticed to a printer, worked as a riverboat pilot until the Civil War closed the river, served briefly in a Confederate militia, and went west to Nevada and California in 1861. 'The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County' (1865) made him famous; The Innocents Abroad (1869), Roughing It (1872), Tom Sawyer (1876) and Huckleberry Finn (1884-85) followed. He married Olivia Langdon in 1870, lost a fortune in the Paige typesetter, and made a world lecture tour in 1895-96. He died at Redding, Connecticut, on 21 April 1910.
literary_profile: Twain wrote American English as it was spoken: his great innovation is the first-person vernacular narrator whose idiom, irony and moral hesitation carry the whole book, and Huckleberry Finn is the founding text of the American novel of voice. He is also the great American satirist of pretension, of the South's romance of itself, and of the 'damned human race', and his late work is one of the darkest bodies of writing in American literature.
stylistic_characteristics: First-person vernacular narration; deadpan comic exaggeration; the tall tale and the shaggy-dog story; ironic understatement; dialect rendered phonetically; the abrupt turn from comedy to horror.
intellectual_concerns: Slavery and the moral conscience of a boy; the Mississippi and the American frontier; the romance of the South and its self-deception; money, speculation and the Gilded Age; imperialism and the Philippine war; death, determinism and the dark side of providence.
historical_significance: Twain is the central American humorist and the founding novelist of American vernacular prose: Huckleberry Finn is the book from which, in Hemingway's phrase, all modern American literature comes, and his influence on American comedy, on the short story and on the literature of race is foundational.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County, and Other Sketches (1867); The Innocents Abroad (1869); Roughing It (1872); The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today (with Charles Dudley Warner, 1873); Sketches New and Old (1875); The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876); A Tramp Abroad (1880); The Prince and the Pauper (1881); Life on the Mississippi (1883); Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884-85); A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court (1889); The American Claimant (1892); Pudd'nhead Wilson (1894); Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc (1896); Following the Equator (1897); The Man That Corrupted Hadleyburg (1900); A Dog's Tale (1904); Extracts from Captain Stormfield's Visit to Heaven (1909); The Mysterious Stranger (1916, posthumous); Autobiography of Mark Twain (2010-, posthumous).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the realist novel and the criticism of fiction
literary_identity: Novelist, critic and editor; the theorist and chief practitioner of American literary realism.
biography: Born at Martins Ferry, Ohio, on 1 March 1837, the son of a printer and newspaper editor; he taught himself the trade and languages, wrote a campaign life of Lincoln in 1860, and was American consul at Venice in 1861-65. He was assistant editor (1866-71) and then editor (1871-81) of the Atlantic Monthly, and from 1886 wrote the 'Editor's Study' for Harper's Monthly, the most influential critical column in America. He wrote some forty novels, including A Modern Instance (1882), The Rise of Silas Lapham (1885) and A Hazard of New Fortunes (1890). He died in New York on 11 May 1920.
literary_profile: Howells made realism the official programme of American fiction: he argued that the novel should concern itself with the ordinary, contemporary and 'smiling aspects' of American life, and his own best novels — the Boston of The Rise of Silas Lapham, the New York of A Hazard of New Fortunes — give the most exact picture we have of the American middle class in the Gilded Age. He was also the most generous and consequential literary editor of his time, the first American champion of Tolstoy, Ibsen and Zola, and the defender of the Haymarket defendants.
stylistic_characteristics: Plain, unobtrusive narrative prose; dialogue that reproduces the hesitations of educated American speech; the detailed interior of the middle-class home; the drama of business and marriage; irony so dry it can be missed; the broad social canvas organised around a single family.
intellectual_concerns: The ethics of business and the making of an American fortune; marriage, divorce and the position of women; the city and the suburban home; class and the immigrant poor; the literary marketplace; socialism and the American conscience after Haymarket.
historical_significance: Howells is the founding theorist of American realism and a major novelist in his own right: his editorial and critical work created the climate in which Twain, James, Crane and Wharton wrote, and The Rise of Silas Lapham and A Hazard of New Fortunes are the central American novels of business and of the Gilded Age city.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Lives and Speeches of Abraham Lincoln and Hannibal Hamlin (1860); Venetian Life (1866); Italian Journeys (1867); Suburban Sketches (1871); Their Wedding Journey (1872); A Chance Acquaintance (1873); A Foregone Conclusion (1875); The Lady of the Aroostook (1879); The Undiscovered Country (1880); A Modern Instance (1882); The Rise of Silas Lapham (1885); Indian Summer (1886); April Hopes (1888); Annie Kilburn (1888); A Hazard of New Fortunes (1890); Criticism and Fiction (1891); The Quality of Mercy (1892); The World of Chance (1893); The Coast of Bohemia (1893); My Literary Passions (1895); The Landlord at Lion's Head (1897); Literary Friends and Acquaintance (1900); The Kentons (1902); The Son of Royal Langbrith (1904); My Mark Twain (1910); Years of My Youth (1916).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American-British; the novel of consciousness and the international theme
literary_identity: Novelist, short-story writer and critic; the greatest American novelist of the later nineteenth century and the master of the psychological novel.
biography: Born in New York on 15 April 1843, the son of the philosopher Henry James Sr and the brother of William James; he was educated in New York, Geneva, London, Paris and Bonn and studied law briefly at Harvard. He settled in London in 1876 and in Rye, Sussex, in 1897, and became a British subject in 1915 in protest at American neutrality. He published Roderick Hudson (1875), The American (1877), The Portrait of a Lady (1881), The Bostonians (1886), The Princess Casamassima (1886), What Maisie Knew (1897), The Wings of the Dove (1902), The Ambassadors (1903) and The Golden Bowl (1904). He died in London on 28 February 1916.
literary_profile: James made the novel a study of consciousness: his late style follows the interior movement of a mind as it perceives, hesitates and revises, and his great subject is the American encounter with European civilisation — the innocent abroad, the heiress and the fortune-hunter, the moral cost of experience. He was also the finest English critic of fiction of the century, and his prefaces to the New York Edition are the founding documents of the modern theory of the novel.
stylistic_characteristics: Long, syntactically suspended sentences with delayed qualification; the 'central consciousness' through which everything is filtered; dialogue that works by indirection and inference; the withheld fact; the elaborate metaphor drawn from architecture, painting or the theatre.
intellectual_concerns: The American and Europe; innocence, experience and the loss of illusions; marriage, money and the marriage market; the artist and society (above all in The Tragic Muse); the woman's consciousness and freedom; betrayal, renunciation and the conduct of life.
historical_significance: James is the central American novelist of the nineteenth century after Melville and the founder of the modern psychological novel: his late novels are the most technically ambitious in English, his criticism is the foundation of narrative theory, and his influence on Woolf, Proust, Conrad and the whole twentieth-century novel is decisive.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: A Passionate Pilgrim and Other Tales (1875); Roderick Hudson (1875); Transatlantic Sketches (1875); The American (1877); French Poets and Novelists (1878); Daisy Miller (1878); The Europeans (1878); Confidence (1879); Hawthorne (1879); Washington Square (1880); The Portrait of a Lady (1881); The Bostonians (1886); The Princess Casamassima (1886); Partial Portraits (1888); The Aspern Papers (1888); The Tragic Muse (1890); The Real Thing and Other Tales (1893); Terminations (1895); Embarrassments (1896); The Other House (1896); What Maisie Knew (1897); The Awkward Age (1899); The Wings of the Dove (1902); The Ambassadors (1903); The Golden Bowl (1904); The American Scene (1907); The New York Edition of the Novels and Tales, 24 vols (1907-09); Notes of a Son and Brother (1914); The Middle Years (1917, posthumous).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the regional sketch and the novel of women's friendship
literary_identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the finest American regionalist of the nineteenth century and the author of The Country of the Pointed Firs.
biography: Born Theodora Sarah Orne Jewett at South Berwick, Maine, on 3 September 1849, the daughter of a country doctor whose rounds gave her the material for her fiction. She published her first story in the Atlantic Monthly in 1869, and Deephaven (1877) established her as a writer of Maine coastal life; she travelled in Europe, was a close friend of Annie Fields, and received an honorary degree from Bowdoin in 1901. She died at South Berwick on 24 June 1909 after a carriage accident.
literary_profile: Jewett wrote the American regional story as a form of delicate social history: her subject is the small Maine port towns after the decline of the shipping trade, and her method is the sketch, the remembered voice and the quiet epiphany rather than plot. Her masterpiece, The Country of the Pointed Firs, has almost no story and yet is one of the most perfectly constructed books in American literature; her treatment of the friendship of women and of the life of unmarried women is unique in her period.
stylistic_characteristics: Episodic sketch structure held together by a visiting narrator; exact rendering of dialect and of old people's speech; precise, unfussy description of coastal houses, herbs and weather; irony and tenderness in balance; the epiphany at the level of a shared silence.
intellectual_concerns: The decay of the New England port towns; the lives of unmarried and elderly women; friendship and community; the sea and the coastal landscape; memory and the local past; the contrast between the summer visitor and the settled inhabitant.
historical_significance: Jewett is the finest American regionalist writer of the century and the most important woman writer of New England after Stowe: The Country of the Pointed Firs is a permanent classic, and its treatment of women's friendships and of the dignity of ordinary lives made her a central figure for the feminist criticism of American literature.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Deephaven (1877); Play Days (1878); Old Friends and New (1879); Country By-Ways (1881); The Mate of the Daylight (1884); A Country Doctor (1884); A Marsh Island (1885); A White Heron and Other Stories (1886); The King of Folly Island (1888); Betty Leicester (1890); Strangers and Wayfarers (1890); A Native of Winby (1893); The Life of Nancy (1895); The Country of the Pointed Firs (1896); The Queen's Twin (1899); The Tory Lover (1901); Verses (1916, posthumous); Letters of Sarah Orne Jewett (1911, posthumous).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the local-colour sketch and the novel of female awakening
literary_identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the author of The Awakening and the finest American writer of Louisiana Creole life.
biography: Born Katherine O'Flaherty in St Louis on 8 February 1850, the daughter of an Irish merchant and a French-Creole mother; she was educated at the Sacred Heart convent and married Oscar Chopin, a cotton factor, in 1870, moving to New Orleans and then to a plantation in Natchitoches Parish. Widowed in 1882, she returned to St Louis and began writing in 1889. Bayou Folk (1894) and A Night in Acadie (1897) made her a successful local colourist; The Awakening (1899) was condemned and she wrote little afterwards. She died in St Louis on 22 August 1904.
literary_profile: Chopin wrote the American short story of sexual and social truth: her Louisiana stories are exact, unsentimental and often very funny about the arrangements between men and women, and The Awakening is the first American novel to treat a woman's sexual and spiritual awakening as its central subject without either condemning or sentimentalising it. Her prose is quiet, exact and entirely free of moralising, which is why it seemed so dangerous.
stylistic_characteristics: Cool, exact, sensory prose; the withheld judgment; the Creole dialect of the Louisiana stories; the short lyric epiphany; the refusal of a moral conclusion; the symbolism of sea, sleep and music.
intellectual_concerns: Marriage and the position of women; female desire and selfhood; Creole and Cajun Louisiana and its racial order; motherhood as an institution rather than an instinct; suicide and freedom; the artist and the woman.
historical_significance: Chopin is the central American woman novelist of the 1890s and the author of the founding American novel of female emancipation: The Awakening was condemned in 1899 and rediscovered in the 1960s, and it is now the key text of American feminist literary criticism and one of the great novels of the century.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: At Fault (1890); Bayou Folk (1894); A Night in Acadie (1897); The Awakening (1899); The Complete Works of Kate Chopin (1969, posthumous); 'The Story of an Hour' (1894); 'Désirée's Baby' (1893); 'A Respectable Woman' (1894); 'The Storm' (written 1898, published 1969).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the feminist treatise, the utopia and the short story
literary_identity: Writer, sociologist and feminist theorist; the author of 'The Yellow Wallpaper' and Women and Economics, and the most systematic American feminist thinker of the century.
biography: Born Charlotte Anna Perkins in Hartford, Connecticut, on 3 July 1860, the great-niece of Harriet Beecher Stowe; she married the artist Charles Walter Stetson in 1884, suffered severe postpartum depression, and was treated by the rest cure of S. Weir Mitchell, which produced 'The Yellow Wallpaper' (1892). She divorced in 1894, supported herself by lecturing and writing, published Women and Economics in 1898, edited the Forerunner (1909-16), and married her cousin George Houghton Gilman in 1900. She died in Pasadena on 17 August 1935.
literary_profile: Gilman wrote the American feminist argument as social science: Women and Economics analyses the economic dependency of women as the root of their subjection, and 'The Yellow Wallpaper' turns the medical treatment of women into the greatest American story of the 1890s. Her utopian fiction — Herland and Moving the Mountain — is the first sustained American feminist utopia, and her cultural criticism is systematic, clear and often startlingly modern.
stylistic_characteristics: Clear, argumentative prose in the service of a thesis; the first-person narrative of mental breakdown; satirical utopia and the reversed anthropology; the sociological essay with statistics and cross-cultural comparison; direct address and repetition.
intellectual_concerns: Women's economic dependency and the case for their paid work; the medical treatment of women and the rest cure; marriage, motherhood and the home as an institution; utopian alternatives; race and the 'woman problem'; work and human dignity.
historical_significance: Gilman is the central American feminist theorist of the nineteenth century after Fuller and a founding figure of the sociology of gender: Women and Economics was translated into seven languages, 'The Yellow Wallpaper' is one of the most studied American stories ever written, and Herland founded the American feminist utopia.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: 'The Yellow Wallpaper' (New England Magazine, 1892); In This Our World (poems, 1893); Women and Economics (1898); Concerning Children (1900); The Home: Its Work and Influence (1903); Human Work (1904); The Man-Made World; or, Our Androcentric Culture (1911); Moving the Mountain (1911); Herland (1915, in the Forerunner); With Her in Ourland (1916); His Religion and Hers (1923); The Living of Charlotte Perkins Gilman: An Autobiography (1935); The Forerunner (editor, 1909-16).

birthplace: Hale's Ford, Franklin County, Virginia, United States
nationality_or_literary_tradition: African-American; the autobiography, the address and the literature of uplift
literary_identity: Educator, orator and writer; the founder of Tuskegee Institute and the most powerful African-American voice of the generation after Reconstruction.
biography: Born into slavery in Franklin County, Virginia, on 5 April 1856; he worked in the salt and coal mines of West Virginia after emancipation, studied at Hampton Institute from 1872, and in 1881 was chosen to head a new normal school at Tuskegee, Alabama, which he built into a major institution. His address at the Atlanta Cotton States Exposition in 1895 made him the spokesman of black America; he advised presidents, founded the National Negro Business League in 1900, and died at Tuskegee on 14 November 1915.
literary_profile: Washington wrote the literature of black self-help: his autobiography, Up from Slavery, is one of the classic American narratives of self-making, and his addresses construct a public philosophy of industrial education, economic advance and accommodation that dominated black American politics for a generation. He is also the central figure in the debate — with W. E. B. Du Bois — over what African-American freedom should mean, and his prose is a masterclass in the rhetoric of indirection.
stylistic_characteristics: First-person narrative of struggle and institutional building; the anecdote as moral lesson; the plain, deliberate sentence; the oratorical cadence of the platform address; conciliation and the calculated omission.
intellectual_concerns: Education, industrial training and self-help; the legacy of slavery and the work of uplift; race relations and the politics of accommodation; the founding and building of institutions; the dignity of labour; the South and the American future.
historical_significance: Washington is the central African-American public figure of the generation after Reconstruction and Up from Slavery is one of the great American autobiographies: his programme built Tuskegee and the black business class, provoked the founding debate of modern black politics, and his autobiography is a permanent document of American self-making.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: The Future of the American Negro (1899); Up from Slavery (1901); 'Atlanta Exposition Address' (1895); The Story of My Life and Work (1900); Working with the Hands (1904); Tuskegee and Its People (1905, editor); The Negro in Business (1907); The Story of the Negro (1909); My Larger Education (1911); Character Building (1902).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: African-American; the short story, the novel of the colour line and the plantation tradition revised
literary_identity: Novelist, short-story writer and lawyer; the first African-American writer of fiction to be published by a major American house, and the most important literary critic of the plantation tradition.
biography: Born in Cleveland, Ohio, on 20 June 1858, but brought up in Fayetteville, North Carolina, where his parents had returned after the Civil War; he taught school, became principal of the State Normal School in Fayetteville, and in 1883 moved to Cleveland, where he studied law and passed the bar. The Conjure Woman (1899) and The Wife of His Youth (1899) were published by Houghton Mifflin; his novels followed, and after 1905 he devoted himself to law and business. He died in Cleveland on 15 November 1932.
literary_profile: Chesnutt wrote the literature of the colour line from inside: his conjure stories use the frame of the old plantation tale in order to undo it, and his novels — The Marrow of Tradition above all — give the first full fictional treatment of the white supremacist terror that ended Reconstruction. He was also the most incisive African-American critic of the plantation tradition and of the publishing industry's demand for minstrel comedy.
stylistic_characteristics: Frame narrative that turns the oral tale against itself; dialect used as a voice of authority rather than comedy; plot built on the legal and social machinery of segregation; satire and irony; exact documentation of the 1898 Wilmington coup in fiction.
intellectual_concerns: Race and the colour line; the legacy of slavery and the failure of Reconstruction; lynching, the Wilmington massacre and white terror; passing and mixed ancestry; the black professional class; the publishing market and the caricature of black life.
historical_significance: Chesnutt is the founding novelist of the African-American literary tradition after Douglass and the most important black American fiction writer before the Harlem Renaissance: The Marrow of Tradition is the first novel about the Wilmington coup of 1898, and The Conjure Woman permanently changed the American short story of race.
